content.text:
Bea borrowed a spool of green string from Mrs. Ives before breakfast.

“Bring it back before supper,” Mrs. Ives said. “It’s the good kind. Doesn’t snap when the wind gets bossy.”

Bea promised. She had a plan for the village welcome festival: a long rainbow of bunting, strung low enough for Rafi, the new boy next door, to help hang it. Last year, the bunting had stretched high over the square, and everyone who helped had needed a ladder. Rafi used a wheelchair. Bea wanted him to tie the last knot himself.

She carried the spool and a stack of paper flags to his house. Rafi was on the front step, folding silver paper into a crescent moon.

“I made a flag,” he said. “It needs a place to fly.”

“Come help me hang the bunting,” Bea said. “No ladders. I brought the string.”

Rafi turned the moon flag in his hands. “Can I choose where it goes?”

“Of course.”

“And tie it?”

“That’s the important part.”

At the square, the festival helpers were setting out jam jars and folding tables. Bea and Rafi started at the gate, stretching the string between two posts at the height of Rafi’s shoulders. Bea knotted one end while Rafi held the spool. They began threading the paper flags onto the line.

Then Mr. Duran came rolling from the bakery with a handcart stacked with bread baskets. He stopped short.

“I can’t get through there,” he called. “The cart needs the gate.”

Bea looked at the string, then at Rafi’s wheels. It crossed the whole entrance, right where everyone would have to pass.

“We could hang it high,” said Mr. Duran. “That’s where it usually goes.”

Bea glanced at the ladder leaning beside the bandstand. She imagined Rafi holding a flag while someone else climbed up to tie it. That wasn’t what she had asked him to come for.

Rafi backed his chair away from the gate. “We need a place where people can roll through,” he said. “And where the flags won’t get caught in anyone’s wheels.”

Mr. Duran waited with his cart. Behind him, more festival helpers were arriving. The welcome arch over the gate stood bare, its old nail holes showing.

Bea untied the string. She had planned to make the biggest rainbow in the village. Now the line was coiled in her hands, and the arch was still empty.

“Let’s use the fence by the welcome table,” she said. “It won’t stretch across the square, but it won’t block anybody.”

Mr. Duran pushed his cart through the gate. “That’ll work,” he said, and rolled on toward the tables.

The fence ran around the little garden beside the welcome table. It was a shorter stretch than the arch, but it had smooth wooden rails and plenty of room to pass. Bea unwound the string along the inside rail. Rafi held the spool steady in his lap and called out when the line began to sag.

“Too loose,” he said.

Bea tugged it tighter.

“Now it’s trying to pull the fence over.”

She laughed and eased it back. Rafi tied a neat knot around the rail, then showed Bea how he had wrapped the string twice before pulling it snug.

“Where should my moon go?” he asked.

“Somewhere it can see the whole festival.”

Rafi chose the middle of the line, beside a yellow paper sun. Bea tied it there. They added flags all along the rail, leaving space between them for the breeze to turn each one.

When they finished, the rainbow curved around the welcome table instead of spanning the square. The gate remained clear. The high arch was still bare.

Mr. Bell, who organized the festival, stopped to look. “We were expecting bunting over the entrance,” he said.

“I know,” Bea replied. Her cheeks felt warm. “But the carts need to get through, and Rafi can reach this.”

Rafi turned his moon so its silver side caught the sun. “It looks better from here,” he said. “You can see every flag.”

Mr. Bell studied the empty arch, then the open gate. He picked up a paper flag from the stack and handed it to a little girl waiting by the table. “Would you like to tie one on?”

Soon, people were stopping to add flags. A baker tied on a tiny loaf. The little girl chose a blue star. Mr. Bell knotted a red square while Rafi showed him the double wrap.

As evening settled, the festival lanterns blinked on. The string held firm along the fence, and the moon flag glimmered between the sun and a paper loaf. Rafi reached down to smooth its pointed tip. Across the clear gate, Mr. Duran rolled the last bread basket into the square. The little girl’s blue star spun in the breeze beside the moon.
